sections.bio:
Sales is what I do, and for the past ten years, I've been working across both structured corporate environments and fast-moving startups. I've built sales teams from scratch and learned how to create Go-To-Market strategies that deliver real results. This journey has taught me a lot about what works (and what doesn’t) in different sales settings and how to adapt to succeed.

Along the way, I've developed the skills to navigate tough sales situations, land big deals, and build processes that drive success. My efforts have paid off—I’ve managed to multiply my salary eightfold over the last five years by applying the same strategies I teach others.

I’ve spent the last 2.5 years building my personal brand and growing an audience of 45k followers. I love collaborating with B2B SaaS companies that appreciate a bit of humor. Check out my posts — I share the daily struggles of salespeople with a lighthearted twist.

posts.text:
Customer problems belong to everyone. 

Sales is fighting fires.
Tech Support is fighting fires.
The Product team is fighting fires.
The customer is caught in the middle.
Then Customer Success walks in with the pizza. 🍕

As a Seller, I’ve learned that customer problems rarely belong to one department.
Sales may close the deal.

Delivering the promised value involves:
Product
Customer Success
Tech / Support
Operations
Leadership

Silos create blame.

Sales blames Product.

Product blames Engineering.

Support blames the customer.

Customer Success tries to fix everything.

The customer thinks:
“Why is this so difficult?”
The best organisations align different departments around the same customer outcome.

Solving customer problems is everyone’s responsibility.

What does this look like in your organisation?

There is a difference between university intelligence and street intelligence.
Look at the math test below. The kid did not solve it the way the teacher wanted. He solved it anyway.
In sales, I meet both types every week.
One knows every framework by heart. MEDDIC, clean discovery, perfect notes in the CRM.
The other one can barely spell MEDDIC, but somehow gets the CFO on a call on a Friday afternoon.
Ten years in, my honest take: frameworks can be taught in two weeks. Finding a way around a closed door cannot.
The best reps I have worked with carry a bit of both. Structure keeps the deal clean. Street smarts keep it alive.
Which skill would you rather have on your team? 👇

Being a salesperson in 2026 is tough. The stack keeps growing and somehow the job gets slower, not faster.

I counted it out one afternoon. CRM in one tab. Sales engagement platform in another. Intent data over here. Enrichment tool over there. A list-building tool in a fifth tab. 

My day had turned into copying a name out of one tool, pasting it into another, exporting a CSV, cleaning it up, importing it somewhere else, and losing my train of thought every single time I switched.

That's the part nobody warns you about. The tools are supposed to save time, but the jumping between them quietly eats your whole day. I was spending more time moving data around than actually talking to buyers.

Then I found out FullEnrich works with Claude, and that changed the whole thing for me.
Now I don't jump between tools. 

I tell Claude what I want, and FullEnrich builds the list for me. No tabs, no exports, no stitching data together by hand. I describe the accounts and people I'm after in plain language, and I get back clean, verified contacts ready to use.

What got me wasn't a feature, it was getting my time back. The hours I used to lose to tab-switching now go into the part of the job that actually matters, which is talking to people and closing deals.

For enterprise sellers, focus is everything. Every minute spent wrangling tools is a minute not spent in front of a buyer.

If you're tired of jumping between tools too, I'll drop the link in the comments for anyone who wants to try it.
#FullEnrichPartner

The fastest way to kill outbound ROI?
 
Leave replies sitting.
 
“Interested” replies get answered the same day. Easy.
 
It’s the objections and curious-but-noncommittal replies that used to sit in my inbox.
 
In enterprise sales, those are often the replies that need the most care.
 
A rushed answer can sound pushy.
 A delayed answer can kill momentum.
 
One thread in particular was an objection that needed context, not another generic “happy to jump on a call” response.
 
Another was simply the wrong contact.
 
Both are easy to leave for later when your inbox is full.
 
Then I found the Reply Draft Assistant from La Growth Machine, a free skill that puts Claude into my reply stage.
 
I point Claude at my LGM inbox, a campaign or a thread I paste in.
 
It reads the conversation, classifies the reply, and drafts an answer matched to the lead’s tone and length.
 
An objection gets a calm response.
 A wrong contact gets a short redirect.
 
I still approve every send.
 
I can tweak drafts with “make it shorter” or “drop the call ask,” and skip replies I want to handle myself.
 
Nothing goes out until I say so.
 
Connect the LGM inbox via the MCP: my inbox processing time is now a fifth of what it used to be, and clearing every overnight reply before 9am is a morning ritual, not a stretch goal.
 
I don’t want AI to reply for me.
 
I want it to reduce the effort while I keep the judgment.
 
How are you making sure the difficult replies don’t sit in your inbox too long?
 
Free skill - link in the comments to test it on your own inbox👇

I used to hide the weak spots of my product during demos. I was wrong.

Early in my career I ran what felt like a perfect demo. Controlled setup, no errors, every click landed exactly where I promised. The prospect signed. Then they logged in themselves and ran straight into a limitation I never mentioned.

That follow-up call was the most uncomfortable conversation of my quarter.

Now I do two things differently. I still demo in a safe environment, because nothing kills momentum faster than a live bug in front of six stakeholders. But I also say out loud what the product cannot do.

What changed for me:

• Prospects believe the parts I praise, because they heard the parts I criticized
• Objections surface during the sales cycle instead of after signature
• Onboarding runs smoother, since expectations were set months before go-live

Naming a limitation has never cost me a deal. Hiding one has. 

If your demo only shows the best case, the surprise does not disappear. It just arrives later, with your name attached to it.

Try it on your next demo. Pick one honest limitation, mention it early, and see how the tone of the conversation changes.
